newsitem.title: EGYPT: Christopher says Mideast peace survives "traumas".
newsitem.headline: Christopher says Mideast peace survives "traumas".

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said on Tuesday that Arabs and Israelis remained committed to forging ahead with the peace process despite the "traumas" that had hit the Middle East in the past year.
He told a Middle East and North African economic conference that for future negotiations to succeed, each side must recognise that there could be no winners or losers.
Christopher said he believed an agreement in current Israeli-Palestinian talks on an Israeli troop deployment in the West Bank town of Hebron was "close at hand".

But his spokesman, Nicholas Burns, advised journalists against expecting a deal in the next few days. He said a 90-minute meeting between Christopher and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat had not shown "any specific progress" on Hebron.

In what is likely to be his last major speech on the Middle East, Christopher, who will step down in January, said there was "no doubt that the peace process has been tested -- tested severely -- by the traumas of the last year".

He was apparently referring to the assassination of Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin a year ago, a string of suicide bombings in Israel by Moslem militants in February and March, and bloody Israeli-Palestinian clashes in September.
"But over the past year, and especially in recent weeks, the peace process has also demonstrated great resilience," the secretary of state said.

"Arabs and Israelis alike know what war means. They have already glimpsed the promise of peace. By looking back into the abyss, both Arabs and Israelis recognised the imperative of moving forward," he said.
He said both Palestinians and Israelis had a "fundamental self-interest" in ending their conflict but understood that it could only be resolved "in phases over time".
Once the Hebron talks finally succeeded, Christopher said he expected the parties to "move ahead with the same sense of urgency to implement the remainder of (their) Interim Agreement".
Israel and the Palestinians have scheduled negotiations due to end by 1999 on the final status of the Palestinian self-rule areas in the West Bank and Gaza, and on Jerusalem.

"For these and future negotiations to succeed, each side must go the extra mile to understand the needs of the other -- to take their requirements into account. Each side must accept that to succeed, there can be no winners or losers," he said.

"Each side must win and be seen to win -- or both sides will lose. Each side must recognise that it is not possible to make peace without taking risks -- but that maintaining the status quo poses even greater risks for the future."

Christopher pledged that U.S. President Bill Clinton, re-elected last week, and the next secretary of state, who has not yet been named, would continue to make Middle East peace a top priority over the next four years.

Summing up the achievements of his four-year tenure, Christopher pointed to two Israeli-Palestinian accords, a peace treaty between Israel and Jordan and growing diplomatic and commercial contacts between Israel and the Arabs.
Alluding to prospects of an agreement between Israel and Syria -- the issue to which he devoted more attention than any other, without avail -- he said only that the opportunity remained.

Christopher said the United States would sign next week the charter of a planned Middle East development bank, and pledged that the Clinton administration would work to win backing from Congress, which has so far denied funds for the project.
